items.title: Real brains follow Dale's principle: a neuron can either excite its neighbors or suppress them, but ...
items.content:
Real brains follow Dale's principle: a neuron can either excite its neighbors or suppress them, but never both. Standard deep learning ignores this and uses backpropagation.

In our new paper, Diffusing Blame, we fix this disconnect. By introducing a routing method that broadcasts error signals directly to the hidden layers, we can train networks made of dedicated positive and negative neurons to strictly obey Dale's principle, all without relying on backprop!

This method works surprisingly well on image recognition tasks despite the strict biological constraints. We also achieved competitive, backprop-free reinforcement learning on complex locomotion tasks and the open-ended Craftax environment.

It is neat to see that representation learning remains possible even when we force deep learning to play by the rules of real neurons.

items.title: So I guess it is time to wonder: how does pre-clearance work for open weights models? No model card ...
items.content:
So I guess it is time to wonder: how does pre-clearance work for open weights models? No model card yet from Kimi K3 but maybe at weight release in a couple weeks, yet open models are easy to jailbreak. Do open models claiming to be Mythos/Sol level (K3 is not yet there, but someone will reach it soon) get vetted by the US/UK/etc? Will China start to care about cyber risk? Since policy has been emergent, I guess no one knows.

And before anyone says you can’t recall open weights models once released, that is true! But governments have levers to require that no company doing business with their nation’s citizens uses unvetted models or serves them, etc. No one is taking away your downloaded weights, but it is entirely possible to make any company avoid using them due to their higher risk.

All of this points to the need for some sort of international cooperation on model vetting.

items.title: New course: Build LLM applications that respond to user requests quickly by running on hardware desi...
items.content:
New course: Build LLM applications that respond to user requests quickly by running on hardware designed for fast inference. This short course was built with  @Cerebras and taught by @zhennydez, @duerr_seb, and  @MilksandMatcha.

When a model generates text, much of the time is spent moving its weights out of memory and into the compute units. Inference-optimized hardware minimizes that movement, making token generation several times faster than on a typical GPU setup. In this course, the hardware you'll use is Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine, which is designed for fast inference by keeping the model's weights close to the compute units.

Fast inference makes lengthy agentic workflows go faster, and also unlocks latency-sensitive, real-time applications like live translation and voice agents.

Skills you'll gain:
- Compare how GPUs, TPUs, and Cerebras' Wafer-Scale Engine each handle the memory-to-compute bottleneck
- Build real-time applications powered by fast inference, including personalizing a webpage and running a multi-step workflow to analyze market signals
- Adopt concrete habits for agentic coding with fast inference, keeping your sessions focused and steering the model more effectively

My teams use Cerebras for several applications that are latency sensitive. Join and build LLM applications that respond quickly:
https://t.co/P8vchGAr22

items.title:
We are pretty screwed with respect to China and LLMs, but it shouldn’t come as a surprise.

I have b...
items.content:
We are pretty screwed with respect to China and LLMs, but it shouldn’t come as a surprise.

I have been trying to warn everyone for a long time. In January 2025 for example, I warned that:

•  the US would not achieve a decisive victory in AI over China if they continued to focus largely on LLMs

• that we would instead converge on a tie

• that the lack of a technical moat would mean that companies like OpenAI would remain unprofitable.

• that Nvidia would be vulnerable 

• that the CHIPS act would backfire, without doing much to hold China back

• that models will continue to get more efficient and less expensive, but that hallucinations and reliability problems will persist.

• that racing endlessly around LLMs would sap resources that could instead go into developing more original ideas.

I wish more people had listened.

items.title: In practice that means giving Claude ways to verify its own work end to end. It means enabling auto ...
items.content:
In practice that means giving Claude ways to verify its own work end to end. It means enabling auto mode for permissions, defaulting on automated code review and security review, and using interfaces that let you manage multiple agents at once (Agent view in CLI, Desktop app, iOS and Android apps, Tag).

To get to higher levels it means /loop, /batch, dynamic workflows, and worktree isolation for subagents. It's not about a single feature, but rather using the right features with the right guardrails that enable Claude to automate entire classes of work in a way that your team can trust the output.

items.title: This week we had a huge global company onsite in SF 🌉 (the company has 2x’ed in size since our last ...
items.content:
This week we had a huge global company onsite in SF 🌉 (the company has 2x’ed in size since our last one!) We solidified our roadmap towards becoming the best document infrastructure for AI agents. We’re building a cracked AI lab focused on all aspects of document work - from document OCR, extraction, search, to e2e workflows - and hillclimbing our capabilities through model training, agent engineering, and deep infrastructure expertise.

We’re also committed to building the most comprehensive, unbiased benchmarks to advance the Pareto frontier for all document tasks. ParseBench has 2k+ enterprise pages, ~80 solutions verified, 15k monthly downloads, and is available across HuggingFace and Kaggle. Next up is increasing our dataset (more verticals) and task coverage (e.g extraction). LlamaParse agentic and cost-effective modes directly define the Pareto curve for VLM-based OCR solutions and we’re making rapid leaps across complex tables, charts, fonts, layouts and more every single day. In addition, liteparse is the fastest, most performant free parser out there and is quickly becoming one of the most popular, eclipsing 11.5k+ stars in ~2 months.

This week we did some work and had a lot of fun. Maybe a little too much fun 😅:
* Spraypainting
* Darts
* Topgolf
* Escape Room
* Soccer
* Many dinners
* Raising Canes for lunch

Time to lock back in. You’re going to see us ship an insane amount of stuff in Q3.

items.title: These guys trained a robot with water bottles, and the robot learned to pick up other objects it had...
items.content:
These guys trained a robot with water bottles, and the robot learned to pick up other objects it had never practiced on.

They did this using reinforcement learning:

1. The robot had to pick a bottle out of a messy tote
2. Then it had to hand the bottle to a person
3. Only water bottles. Nothing else.

After they finished training, they tested the robot on different objects:

• On bottles, the success went from 80% to 98%
• On snack cans, the robot's throughput rose 40%
• On soft bags, the robot's performance improved by 13% even though they're deformable and much harder to handle than rigid objects.

Snack cans and soft bags have different shapes and weights, and the robot was never trained on them.

This was just one of three use cases they tested.

Every hour we spend teaching a robot costs a ton of money. If they only get better at handling the one object they practice on, reinforcement learning will never be worth doing.

But if the gains carry over, we could focus on teaching the hardest possible tasks and let the robot apply that knowledge elsewhere.

Here is the full write-up by @TheHumanoidAI on the infrastructure they used and what they learned:

https://t.co/bslHUyjAGy

Hyperagent's ability...
items.content:
Founders: I built you a YC application reviewing agent with @hyperagentapp.   

Hyperagent's ability to quickly create agents to do a variety of things is pretty darn cool.   

This took me 13 minutes start to finish. 

Thanks to my friend Jeff Stevens who let me run his slide deck through my new agent.   

In the video below I give you some of my own thoughts about @YCombinator and @paulg and what they look for. 

I've been following YC since the beginning, was at its first Startup Schools and have interviewed many YC founders over the years.   

It's all about clarity and traction. Which my new agent will help you with too. It'll review your application and your slide deck and give you feedback about where your company is strong or weak for a YC application.   13 minutes. Nuts.   

Here's the prompt I used:  

"Build an agent called Paul Graham Brain, a YC application reviewer. The user pastes in their pitch deck or memo as text. The agent reviews it the way Paul Graham and a Y Combinator partner would, using its knowledge of Paul Graham's essays and strong YC applications as the standard. It rewrites the pitch in his sharper, clearer style, and it scores the application with honest reasons for the score. No external tools or connections needed. The user pastes their pitch, and it returns the rewrite and the score."  

And in the video here you see how it works.

items.title: Getting this one thing wrong could cost you your business: thinking your company is ahead in AI when...
items.content:
Getting this one thing wrong could cost you your business: thinking your company is ahead in AI when it isn't.

I see it constantly. CEOs shooting themselves in the foot through overconfidence.

It’s not just tools - yes, if you have 100K employees and Copilot is on 10 desks, that’s clearly behind. But it’s also culture. Incentives. Governance. Who actually has permission to build.

I've spent every day of the last decade advising businesses - big and small - through AI transformations. Over that time, I built my own AI-First Index to quickly gauge whether they were trailblazers or stragglers. 

And until now, it was private and only for my clients.

items.content:
My robot is driving me to a robot company in San Francisco.

Life is good! Hope you have a great weekend.

One thing about having a robot to drive you: you will drive more.

I wouldn’t drive the three hour round trip from my house in San Jose nearly as often if I had to manually drive.

So as more people get robots to drive them traffic will get worse.

Which is why Elon is digging tunnels.

All technologies have pros and cons.

I like hanging out with the people who see the pros.

@jacksonaltonh Nice to see Aaron again.

What people aren't seeing is that there's a whole raft of new jobs being created, keeping those who are expert at AI very busy. Even if you look at startups—which is where most job creation comes from—you can have a single-person company run on AI, but who goes to the conferences and sets up the booth?

There are a lot of jobs created around businesses that people aren't really accounting for, so it's good to hear Aaron talk on this.

If non-US citizen: buy VUAA on LS...
items.content:
Open an IBKR account, then buy:

**S&P500**
If US citizen: buy VOO
If non-US citizen: buy VUAA on LSEETF (search VUAA on IBKR)

**Tech**
If you want more tech exposure (more gains but more risk), if US buy QQQ, if non-US buy XUTC

**Bonds**
If you want to keep some money safe put it in bonds, but that also has an ETF, if US buy SGOV, if non-US buy IB01

**Commodities** (e.g. materials)
Want gold? If US buy IAU, non-US by RMAU

**Why difference US vs non-US citizen investing?**
It's cheaper: Irish-domiciled UCITS ETFs generally pay 15% US withholding tax on dividends from US companies, compared to 30% for funds without equivalent treaty access

The only proven thing in investment is that diversification works, you have less gains but less risk, ask AI how to build a nice mix of ETFs, bonds, commodities, real estate/land (p.s. ETFs are categorized as stocks cause they're just a basket of stocks), generally you want to not buy individual stocks with most of your money because it's super volatile and you're betting. It can go both ways, I bet NVIDIA in 2022 and made lots of money but I also bet Alibaba before Jack Ma was arrested and lost 90%!

This is not financial advice

The theory is nothing. AuroraGPT advances scientific discov...
items.content:
AuroraGPT - Built by Scars of Frontline

The theory is nothing. AuroraGPT advances scientific discovery by building generalizable, foundation-scale large-language models across multiple scientific domains, including physics, chemistry, mathematics, and material sciences. In a world dominated by theoretical models and theoritic ideals, AuroraGPT was never born from theoretical laboratory conditions. AuroraGPT forged its foundation in the real-world challenges of exascale computing. Traditional machine learning models operate in narrowly defined, well-structured environments. However, AuroraGPT goes beyond static datasets into domains where mathematics, programming, and extreme complexity dominate. Its architecture generalizes across scientific disciplines, enabling adaptation to evolving scientific data. It also enables faster, scalable, predictive modeling that can adapt to changing scientific data — something conventional models struggle to accomplish at meaningful resolution or exascale computing.

Achieving these objectives required AuroraGPT to survive in the harshest computational environments ever encountered—the early volatile stages of the Aurora Supercomputer. Building at exascale demanded fault-tolerant training algorithms capable of surviving node dropouts, managing inconsistent interconnect bandwidths, and recovering from partial model convergence failures. AuroraGPT’s foundation large language model scaling strategy involved distributing training across 60,000 GPUs while dynamically re-optimizing tensor parallelism, complex mathematics, data parallelism, and pipeline parallelism in fluctuating infrastructure stability. AuroraGPT engineered its resilience mechanisms in direct response to real-world node failures, memory bottlenecks, and system fragmentation — scars from computational battles that ultimately forged a new class of singularity-resilient AI infrastructure.

items.content_html:
AuroraGPT - Built by Scars of Frontline

The theory is nothing. AuroraGPT advances scientific discovery by building generalizable, foundation-scale large-language models across multiple scientific domains, including physics, chemistry, mathematics, and material sciences. In a world dominated by theoretical models and theoritic ideals, AuroraGPT was never born from theoretical laboratory conditions. AuroraGPT forged its foundation in the real-world challenges of exascale computing. Traditional machine learning models operate in narrowly defined, well-structured environments. However, AuroraGPT goes beyond static datasets into domains where mathematics, programming, and extreme complexity dominate. Its architecture generalizes across scientific disciplines, enabling adaptation to evolving scientific data. It also enables faster, scalable, predictive modeling that can adapt to changing scientific data — something conventional models struggle to accomplish at meaningful resolution or exascale computing.

Achieving these objectives required AuroraGPT to survive in the harshest computational environments ever encountered—the early volatile stages of the Aurora Supercomputer. Building at exascale demanded fault-tolerant training algorithms capable of surviving node dropouts, managing inconsistent interconnect bandwidths, and recovering from partial model convergence failures. AuroraGPT’s foundation large language model scaling strategy involved distributing training across 60,000 GPUs while dynamically re-optimizing tensor parallelism, complex mathematics, data parallelism, and pipeline parallelism in fluctuating infrastructure stability. AuroraGPT engineered its resilience mechanisms in direct response to real-world node failures, memory bottlenecks, and system fragmentation — scars from computational battles that ultimately forged a new class of singularity-resilient AI infrastructure.

This is the type of application I've already built earlier at the beginning of this year for a conference demonstration! 

GPT Paper-Reader, to show how you can leverage the summarization capabilities of large language models to retrieve research papers from databases, summarize their content, and engage in Q&A interactions with people.    The future is here.  In addition to the regular theoretical presentation, I'll be presenting a practical GPT. This application utilizes GPT, to effectively read and analyze complete academic papers:  Basically the app chunks the PDF paper into manageable sections for detailed reading and generates concise summaries for each segment. By maintaining context from previous sections within the token limit, it enhances comprehension. Before diving into the paper, you can outline specific questions in the prompt. This approach allows GPT to extract the most important information during its reading and summarizing process, leading to superior outcomes.   After summarizing all parts, you will receive comprehensive answers to your inquiries based on the consolidated summaries. By default, the initialized prompt will target essential points such as:  These inquiries are tailored for research articles within the computer science domain. Upon completion of the paper review, feel free to engage with the question() interface to ask further questions.

items.content:
Generational Performance!  Ruger (The Next Generation of America’s Favorite Hunting Rifle). 

Ruger redefined performance with its bolt-action American Rifle. This year, the company unveiled the enhanced American Rifle Generation, incorporating customer insights and technological innovation for an even better shooting experience. 

The barreled action boasts a striking and durable Cerakote finish. The medium-contour, cold-hammer-forged barrel, featuring deep spiral flutes on most versions (depending on chambering), achieves a balance of reduced weight and maintained accuracy while effectively dissipating heat. Additionally, threaded muzzles and radial-port muzzle brakes are standard on most versions. 

The synthetic stock, featuring a gray splatter finish, can be customized using a removable comb riser and length-of-pull spacers to accommodate various optics and shooter statures. With the ability to add or remove spacers, the length of pull can be adjusted from 12 inches to 13 3/4 inches. Additional comb-height options are available as accessories. Moreover, the soft rubber recoil pad collapses progressively to reduce felt recoil, while Ruger’s patented Power Bedding integral bedding-block system secures the receiver and free-floats the barrel to enhance accuracy.

The second-generation American Rifle is equipped with an enlarged bolt-handle knob for effortless in-the-field bolt action. Additionally, the handle is threaded (5/16”-24) for convenient replacement of the knob. The piece bolt, CNC-machined from stainless steel, features a three-lug, 70-degree throw, ensuring optimal scope clearance.

The rifle is equipped with a position tang safety, which locks the bolt when placed in the rearmost setting, preventing unintentional opening. In the middle position, the rifle can be loaded with the safety engaged. Additionally, the Ruger Marksman Adjustable trigger provides a crisp release with a user-adjustable pull weight ranging up to pounds. 

The rifle offers a versatile chambering, accommodating a variety of cartridges from .22 ARC to 7 mm PRC, and also includes options for straight-wall cartridges. It comes equipped with one magazine and a factory-installed, one-piece Picatinny scope base. Additionally, users have the option to enhance the rifle's balance and recoil absorption by utilizing the accessory stock-weight kit, which can add up to 1.6 pounds to the butt of the rifle.
